bakeLead: The scene is computed once, as fast as possible, and stored in this browser. Then it plays back smoothly — and from every resume point you can go on computing live.
bakeGpuNote: The graphics card bakes many times faster. Its recording cannot be repeated bit for bit, and “Live from here” resumes from the last resume point before the frame. Recordings from the processor and the graphics card are kept side by side.
bakeCpuNote: The processor computes exactly and repeatably — “Live from here” resumes at exactly the frame shown.
bakeCpuOnly: The processor bakes this scene: the graphics card does not compute carved ice, salt grains or more than eight moving bodies yet.
bakeNearCap: That is almost all the space for recordings in this browser (600 MB) — older recordings will be removed.
bakeOverCap: That is more than the space for recordings in this browser (600 MB) — shorten the recording or choose fewer resume points or a coarser grid.
bakeNoWebgpu: This browser has no WebGPU — the processor bakes.
bakeGpuFailed: The graphics card did not start — the processor bakes.
bakeGpuLost: The graphics card stopped responding — what is already baked is saved.

clipFromCpu: This recording was baked by the processor.
clipFromGpu: This recording was baked by the graphics card.
clipToCpu: Show the processor’s recording (at the same moment).
clipToGpu: Show the graphics card’s recording (at the same moment).

title: 2D lab
accelTitle: Open the accelerated view: the whole model runs on the graphics card (WebGPU), on a 1 mm grid.
accelNoOther: The accelerated view does not know carved ice (several rectangles), salt grains, more than eight moving bodies or more than 128 body contacts at once yet — this scene runs in the normal view.

fateBurst: This bubble reached the surface and burst — its vapour escaped into the air. Below is its last state.
fateCollapsed: This bubble vanished: its vapour condensed in the cooler water. Below is its last state.
fateMerged: This bubble merged with another one — the merged bubble is shown now.
whyRise: Why does the bubble rise? The water pushes harder from below than from above (buoyancy) — and vapour weighs almost nothing.
aboutLead: Every model simplifies reality — that is a lesson too. Here is what this model leaves out or approximates.

ai.aiFormat:
Scene “2D lab” — JSON. The engine computes everything from the laws of physics and the materials database; the scene only says what stands where at the start (the starting setup, not the course of events).
Units: metres (origin in the lower left corner of the inside of the box, y upwards), temperatures in °C, pressure in kPa, power in W (per layer thickness).

{ "format": "recreatio/lab2d", "version": 1, "seed": number (repeatable randomness),
  "box": { "w": width (0.2), "h": height (0.15), "depth": thickness of the 2D layer (0.01) },
  "ambient": { "p": kPa (101.325), "T": °C, "rh": humidity 0–1, "g": m/s² (from 2.45 to 19.6), "air": { "N2": 0.7676, "O2": 0.2324 } },
  "sides": { "left" | "right" | "bottom" | "top": "wall" or "open" (an open side is the room) },
  "quality": "high" (2 mm cells, usual) | "very-high" (1 mm) | "medium" (3 mm),
  "extremes": "ask" (default: the lab asks when boiling turns violent) | "compute" (compute exactly — superheated water may boil explosively) | "normalize" (soften — calm boiling), optional,
  "ops": [ build steps in order ] }

Objects — "body" (block, ice cube, stone), "beaker", "hotplate" — have a name "id" (e.g. "cube", "beaker"; without one they get "body-1", "beaker-1" …) and their own settings: "pinned" (stays put, does not fall), "T", "angle", material, size, heating. A setting is changed in the object itself, not in a separate step.

Steps ("op"):
  { "op": "fill", "region": region, "composition": { "H2O": 1 }, "phase": "liquid", "T": °C } — liquid in the region: "H2O" (water) or "oil-rapeseed" (rapeseed oil; does not evaporate, lighter than water, thicker in motion); several liquids at once (mass fractions) spread evenly and separate under gravity; "NaCl" (table salt) dissolves in water: { "H2O": 0.9, "NaCl": 0.1 } is 10 % brine (saturated is about 26 %; the excess crystallises as a crust on the bottom, brine boils above 100 °C); "phase": "gas" with { "N2": 0.7676, "O2": 0.2324 } — air
  { "op": "erase", "region": region } — removes water, bubbles, crystals and solids; room air comes back
  { "op": "grains", "region": region, "material": "NaCl", "d": crystal diameter in m (0.0005 — table salt; from 0.00005 to 0.005), "T": °C } — a handful of salt crystals (loosely poured): falls, sinks in water the slower the finer the crystals (water drag), forms a heap with slopes of about 34°, dissolves where the water is not saturated (cooling it slightly; without stirring the salty water stays at the bottom), in saturated brine the crystals grow; in superheated water the air in the cracks of the crystals triggers sudden boiling
  { "op": "move", "id": object name, "dx": m, "dy": m } — moves an object together with what lies inside its outline (water and bubbles in a beaker, an ice cube in it); this is how a drag with the “Select” tool is recorded. Or { "op": "move", "region": region, "dx", "dy" } — everything solid in the region (a painted structure, by whole cells)
  { "op": "remove", "id": object name } — takes an object away
  { "op": "solid", "region": region, "material": "glass" | "steel" | "ceramic" | "wood" | "ice" | "stone", "T": °C } — a fixed structure made of grid cells (ceramic = boiling chips; ice as a structure does not melt — melting ice is a "body")
  { "op": "body", "id": name, "region": region, "material": "wood" | "ice" | "stone" | "glass" | "steel" | "ceramic", "T": °C, "pinned": true (optional: pinned, stays put), "angle": degrees (optional, rotation about the centre) } — an object: an exact rectangle (a circle becomes a square of the same area, a polygon the rectangle enclosing it, a line with width a rotated rectangle); a free one falls, floats, sinks and tips over (wood 510 kg/m³ floats, ice 917 kg/m³ floats almost fully submerged, stone sinks); ice melts when it is warm and freezes on in water colder than its freezing point — it stays a rectangle, a whole face recedes or grows; in brine it melts below 0 °C (a freezing mixture)
  { "op": "beaker", "id": name, "x": centre, "y": bottom, "w": width, "h": height, "wall": wall thickness, "material": "glass", "T": °C, "lid": true (optional, tight lid), "pinned": false (optional: a free beaker — it may tip over), "angle": degrees (optional, rotation about the centre of the bottom) } — a beaker (cross-section); without "pinned": false it stands pinned
  { "op": "hotplate", "id": name, "x": centre, "y": bottom, "w", "h", "material": "steel", "mode": "power" | "thermostat", "power": W, "target": °C, "on": true, "T": °C, "pinned": false (optional) } — a hot plate (pinned unless "pinned": false)
Region: { "rect": [x0, y0, x1, y1] } | { "circle": [x, y, r] } | { "poly": [[x, y], …] } | { "line": [x0, y0, x1, y1], "width": thickness }
A liquid must have a free surface (gas above it) — a completely flooded closed region is rejected.
ai.aiPrompt:
Prepare a JSON starting setup for the “2D lab” module in REcreatio (a school sandbox: heat, boiling, evaporation, fog, water, oil and brine, salt crystals that sink and dissolve, bodies that fall, float and sink, ice that melts and freezes on).
Topic: [describe what should stand in the box, e.g. “a beaker of hot water on a hot plate, boiling chips on the bottom”].
Rules: real sizes (beaker 7 cm wide, plate 12 cm), things do not overlap, apparatus stands on the bottom (y = 0) or on another thing, water inside the beaker above its bottom; a free object may hang above the water — it will fall (unless it has "pinned": true). Give objects short "id" names. Return ONE JSON object, without comments.

flatWorld.title: Flat world
flatWorld.primary: The box is flat like the pane of a 1 cm thick aquarium. Nothing flows forwards or backwards.
flatWorld.secondary: A 2D layer of thickness D = 1 cm; the front and back walls give off no heat. Bubbles are spheres while they are narrower than the layer, then discs.

grid.title: Grid of 1–3 mm
grid.primary: Temperature and pressure are computed in 2 mm cells. Things smaller than a cell are approximated.
grid.secondary: Fields on 1–3 mm cells; the thin boundary layer at the walls is not resolved — it is replaced by the contact temperature T_f = (k_s T_s + k_l T_l)/(k_s + k_l).

waterAirApart.title: Water and air apart
waterAirApart.primary: Water and air are computed separately: to the water the air is only a pressure, to the air the water is a moving wall.
waterAirApart.secondary: Two separate pressure projections (density ratio ~830 : 1); air trapped in water is not modelled (MultiFLIP is the way forward).

noSound.title: No sound
noSound.primary: There are no sound waves and no explosions in this model.
noSound.secondary: Low Mach number gas: density from temperature and composition at the region pressure p0.

incompressible.title: Water does not compress
incompressible.primary: Water cannot be compressed, but warm water is lighter and rises.
incompressible.secondary: Projection with constant density and gravity g·ρ(T)/ρ_ref — buoyancy from the true density, with its maximum at 4 °C.

tensionInBubbles.title: Surface tension only in bubbles
tensionInBubbles.primary: Drops and the meniscus are not shaped by surface tension. That is why gravity is at least 1/4 of Earth’s.
tensionInBubbles.secondary: The capillary length of water (~2.7 mm) is about one cell; surface tension acts in the bubble models (pressure inside, nucleation, detachment).

noRadiation.title: No radiation
noRadiation.primary: Heat flows by contact and motion, not by glowing.
noRadiation.secondary: No thermal radiation: a very hot plate loses less heat than it really would.

lossesOneNumber.title: Losses as one number
lossesOneNumber.primary: The room behind the box is not computed — the walls lose heat according to one number.
lossesOneNumber.secondary: h_ext = 10 W/(m²·K) on the walls of the box, in series with half a cell.

cavities.title: Pits in the walls
cavities.primary: Bubbles are born in tiny pits in the walls. Boiling chips have many large ones.
cavities.secondary: Up to 8 cavities per wall cell, radii from a power-law distribution (steel after Lemmert and Chawla); activation at T_f − T_sat ≥ ΔT_act.

bubbleFormulas.title: Bubbles from formulas
bubbleFormulas.primary: Growth, detachment and motion of bubbles are computed by formulas tested in laboratories (accurate to about 10–20 %).
bubbleFormulas.secondary: Growth: Plesset–Zwick and Ranz–Marshall; detachment: Fritz; drag: Tomiyama (contaminated water); no lift force and no collisions other than merging.

idealGases.title: Ideal gases
idealGases.primary: Air is nitrogen and oxygen; vapour behaves like an ideal gas.
idealGases.secondary: The enthalpy of vapour depends only on T; the heat of vaporisation away from 100 °C follows Kirchhoff’s law (0.5 % too low at 20 °C).

fogNoFall.title: Fog does not settle
fogNoFall.primary: Fog flows with the air and does not fall like rain.
fogNoFall.secondary: Fog is a mass per cell carried with the gas; dew settles only on the walls.

liquidsOneFlow.title: Several liquids, one flow
liquidsOneFlow.primary: Water and oil flow in a shared velocity field; each liquid has its own density, so oil floats on water.
liquidsOneFlow.secondary: Projection with a constant (mean) density, gravity from the density of each particle — hydrostatics exact in every layer, inertia approximate (good for density ratios of about 0.7–1.5).

viscosity.title: Viscosity only where it matters
viscosity.primary: Oil flows “thickly”, water almost without friction — because in 2 mm cells the friction of water is negligible.
viscosity.secondary: Viscosity computed implicitly in the simplified form ∇·(η∇u), only when the scene holds a liquid other than water; the liquid sticks to the walls, the free surface has no stress.

subcellDrops.title: Drops smaller than a cell
subcellDrops.primary: A droplet of oil in water (or of water in oil) rises or sinks at the speed a real drop of that size would have.
subcellDrops.secondary: A particle surrounded by another liquid drifts at the terminal velocity of a drop of its volume (Schiller–Naumann drag, Hadamard–Rybczynski correction). There is no tension between the liquids — drops are not round, and an emulsion separates faster than a real fine one.

onlyWaterEvaporates.title: Only water evaporates
onlyWaterEvaporates.primary: Oil does not evaporate, smoke or burn. A vapour bubble in oil simply passes through it.
onlyWaterEvaporates.secondary: Oil has no vapour pressure in the model; a vapour bubble in oil neither grows nor condenses; oil data measured at 20–160 °C, extrapolated above.

saltInWater.title: Salt in water
saltInWater.primary: Salt dissolved in water raises the boiling point and lowers the freezing point. All of it follows from one quantity: the water activity.
saltInWater.secondary: Water activity from the Pitzer equations (PHREEQC parameters, below 0 °C Spencer–Møller–Weare): vapour pressure over brine a_w·p_sat, boiling at a_w·p_sat(T_b) = p, freezing from the equilibrium with ice. Density and specific heat of brine after Laliberté. Salts other than NaCl: later stages.

saltMixing.title: Salt mixes when the water flows
saltMixing.primary: Salty and fresh water brought together in one cell by the flow even out within seconds while the water flows, and within minutes while it stands still. Between cells salt spreads by itself very slowly — millimetres per hour; further on, the moving water carries it.
saltMixing.secondary: Ion diffusion: D = 1.61·10⁻⁹ m²/s at 25 °C (Nernst–Hartley mean), at other temperatures after Stokes–Einstein. In still water every particle approaches the mean salt content of its cell with the time τ = Δx²/(π² D) (4.8 min at 2 mm and 20 °C). Flowing water stretches what is in the cell into ever thinner bands (stretching λ) — salt diffuses quickly across a thin band: mixing time t = W(2λτ)/(2λ) (W — Lambert function; Ranz 1979, Villermaux 2019), 2.4 s at λ = 1/s. Between cells Fick’s law. D does not depend on concentration here (in reality it drops by about 8 % at 1 mol/kg).

crystalsOnBottom.title: Crystals straight onto the bottom
crystalsOnBottom.primary: When water goes away and the solution is saturated, the excess salt settles at once as a white crust on the nearest wall below — or grows on a salt crystal lying nearby. The crust does not dissolve again.
crystalsOnBottom.secondary: The excess above solubility (Pitzer, Peiper and Busey 1984) passes at once onto a crystal in the same or a neighbouring cell, and without one into a crust on the nearest solid cell (no supersaturation; no new crystals form in the liquid); the heat of crystallisation stays in the liquid. The crust does not dissolve back — only crystals dissolve.

roundGrains.title: Salt crystals as round grains
roundGrains.primary: Poured salt is crystals, but in the model one grain stands for many real ones, is round and does not roll. Friction is chosen so that a heap of salt has slopes of about 34° — like real fine salt.
roundGrains.secondary: Grain particles (each standing for N crystals of diameter d, four per cell at a packing of 0.58) are discs without rotation; contact and friction (static μ = 0.245, kinetic 0.2) as position constraints (PBD, Macklin et al. 2014), lower grains count as heavier — the heap stands at once. The angle of repose of fine salt, 34 ± 3°, is a cited value (no measurement for 0.3–0.8 mm); a single heap scatters by ±2°. Grains take space from the water but not from the air.

saltSinks.title: Salt sinks and dissolves
saltSinks.primary: Crystals sink in water as fast as real ones of that size and dissolve only where the water is not yet saturated — dissolving cools the water slightly. In superheated water a bubble is born on every dry crystal.
saltSinks.secondary: Settling velocity after Ferguson and Church (2004), implicit drag, force passed to the water; density and temperature from the water particles in the grain’s cell, viscosity of pure water (saturated brine has almost twice as much). Dissolution ṁ = A k ρ ln(1 + B), k = Sh D/d, Sh = 1 + (1 + Re·Sc)^⅓ f(Re) (Clift et al.); salt enters the water with the enthalpy of the crystal (heat of solution +4.6 kJ/mol at 20 °C, negative at 100 °C). The cracks of dry crystals hold air: they act like a wall cavity with a radius of 10 µm (about 3.3 K of superheat) and give a bubble at most every 25 ms — for 2 s in water, then they are flooded (model assumptions).

airDroplets.title: Droplets in the air
airDroplets.primary: A splash or a leftover of water smaller than a cell boils when it is hotter than the boiling point, but below it does not evaporate.
airDroplets.secondary: Particles in a cell that is not liquid: above T_boil they evaporate into their cell (a drop that evaporated completely leaves its salt as a crust), two cells away from the liquid they fly ballistically; there is no evaporation below T_boil — a drop on a cold wall does not dry.

iceWholeWalls.title: Ice melts by whole faces
iceWholeWalls.primary: An ice cube melts when it is warm and freezes onto itself in cold water — but it stays a rectangle: a whole face recedes or grows at once, and the corners stay sharp. Water away from ice does not freeze, even when very cold.
iceWholeWalls.secondary: Heat inside the ice above the melting point passes at once to the face through which heat flows in (water, air, hot plate) and moves it evenly; water colder than T_f in front of the face freezes on. The front lies in cells: first-order accuracy in Δx — the Neumann solution within 6–7 % at 2 mm. Ice forms only on ice (no nucleation and no frost); vapour pressure below 0 °C as at 0 °C. Water from under a cube lying on the plate flows out at its two edges (there is no water film under the cube), and the last quarter of an ice cell melts in one step.

heatInCell.title: Heat evens out within a cell
heatInCell.primary: A hot and a cold water particle in the same cell even out their temperature within seconds — as fast as water conducts.
heatInCell.secondary: The grid conducts heat between cells; within a cell every particle approaches the mean temperature of the cell with the time τ = Δx²/(π² α), α = k/(ρ c_p) (water at 20 °C: 2.8 s at 2 mm, 0.7 s at 1 mm; IEM model) — in flowing water too: faster evening out in the cell would carry the heat of a hot wall into the neighbouring cells, and the water at the boiling chips would be too cold. The energy of the cell stays exactly the same; a drop alone in the air exchanges no heat with others.

roomBehindSide.title: The room behind an open side
roomBehindSide.primary: Behind an open side there is ordinary room air.
roomBehindSide.secondary: Inflow brings ambient air; what flows out is counted as “escaped”.

rigidBodies.title: Bodies as wholes
rigidBodies.primary: A beaker, a plate, a wooden block or an ice cube are rigid wholes: pinned they stay put, unpinned they fall, float, sink and tip over. Wood floats half submerged, ice almost completely. A body floating in a small vessel rocks slightly (by less than a cell).
rigidBodies.secondary: A body is a few exact rectangles (they lie between cells and at an angle; each of their inner cells has its own energy) with position, velocity, mass and moment of inertia; collisions as in Physics 2D (SAT, warm start, Coulomb friction). The grid sees the body as fractions covering the cells and their faces, so buoyancy changes smoothly with position. The force of water and air is the pressure on the true outline; the mass of water moved with the body is measured by an extra solve of the pressure projection. A gap narrower than half a cell is not seen: a cell covered by 99 % (by an unpinned body already by 90 %) counts as full, and a small air pocket (under 2 cm³) closed only by an unpinned body counts as open — its air escapes. A falling square has too little drag (C_D about 1.8 instead of 2.1), because its wake has no time to shed alternately.

frictionlessWalls.title: Walls without friction
frictionlessWalls.primary: Water slides along the walls without friction. At a real wall a thin film of water stands still.
frictionlessWalls.secondary: Free slip at the walls (mirrored nodes in APIC): the boundary layer is much thinner than a cell.

onlyBubbles.title: Only bubbles in water
onlyBubbles.primary: No empty spaces can form inside water — gas in water is only bubbles.
onlyBubbles.secondary: A cell becomes gas only when it was gas or borders gas: there is no cavitation and no air bubbles entrained by splashing. Gas that would still remain in a cell with water (e.g. vapour from a bubble that collapsed where there is no water any more) passes at once to the nearest cell with air.

violentBoiling.title: Violent boiling
violentBoiling.primary: A very hot wall gives bubbles at most as much heat as real boiling lets through. With “Soften” boiling is calmer than in reality: large bubbles escape into the air at once, and water does not fly out of the vessel. “Ask” pauses the simulation when boiling turns violent.
violentBoiling.secondary: Heat to a bubble on the wall limited by the critical heat flux q″ = 0.149 ρ_v^½ h_lv [σ g (ρ_l − ρ_v)]^¼ (Lienhard and Dhir 1973; 1.26 MW/m² at 1 atm); there is no transition or film boiling (Leidenfrost). A bubble larger than a cell is still an object: it pushes water away by its volume fraction and a ring of water around it, and does not deform. “Soften”: 1/10 of the flux, nucleation at the latest at 2 K of superheat, bubbles at most 4 mm (the rest goes to the air), water at most 1.5 m/s — with exact mass and energy.

tinyBubbles.title: Many tiny bubbles
tinyBubbles.primary: At a hot bottom more tiny bubbles are born than in reality; most of them vanish at once.
tinyBubbles.secondary: One wall cell (2 mm) holds the whole superheat at the wall, so a cavity is ready again quickly; in subcooled water thousands of bubbles per second are born and collapse. The energy is right, the number of bubbles is too high.

fogWhiteness.title: How white the fog is
fogWhiteness.primary: Fog is drawn as if you were looking through the whole beaker, not through a thin 1 cm layer.
fogWhiteness.secondary: Opacity from the Beer–Lambert law for droplets with a radius of 1.5 µm along a path of 7 cm. The amount of fog is computed, its whiteness is an assumption.
